concepts.def: The theory that cells are the basic structural unit of all living organisms: every living organism consists of one or more cells, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Because it is a general theory, it can be used to make predictions about organisms that have not yet been examined.

Reasoning from a general theory to a specific prediction that can then be tested by observation. From cell theory, a biologist can deduce that a newly discovered organism will consist of one or more cells before it has been examined under a microscope. Deduction runs from the general to the particular; induction runs the other way, from many particular observations to a general statement.

How many times larger an image is than the object it shows: magnification = size of image ÷ actual size of object, with both sizes converted to the same units before dividing. Rearranged, actual size = size of image ÷ magnification. Magnification has no units and is written as, for example, ×400.

An eyepiece graticule is a scale of equally spaced divisions fitted inside the eyepiece, so it appears superimposed on the specimen. It has no fixed value in micrometres: it must be calibrated for each objective lens by lining it up with a stage micrometer, a slide carrying a scale of known length (for example 100 µm divided into 100 divisions of 1 µm). Once the value of one graticule division is known for that objective, the actual size of a specimen is the number of divisions it spans multiplied by that value.

A line drawn on a micrograph or drawing that represents a stated actual length in the specimen, for example 10 µm. Its drawn length equals the actual length it represents multiplied by the magnification, so a 10 µm scale bar on a ×2000 image is 20 000 µm (20 mm) long. A scale bar allows actual sizes to be judged directly from the image without stating the magnification.

A temporary mount is a specimen placed in a drop of water or stain on a slide and covered with a coverslip for immediate viewing. Most cell structures are almost transparent, so stains such as iodine solution or methylene blue are used to increase contrast between structures; a stain does not increase magnification or resolution.

The two focusing controls of a light microscope. The coarse adjustment moves the stage or objective through large distances and is used only with the low-power objective to bring the specimen roughly into focus. The fine adjustment moves through very small distances and is used to sharpen the image, and is the only control used with high-power objectives, where the lens is close to the slide and coarse movement could break the slide or damage the lens.

An observation that produces a numerical value, such as measuring the length of a cell in graticule divisions or in micrometres. Measurement using instruments such as a calibrated microscope is a form of quantitative observation, as opposed to a qualitative observation, which describes without measuring.

The smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate. Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used: visible light gives a light microscope a resolution of about 200 nm, whereas an electron beam has a far shorter wavelength and gives an electron microscope a resolution below 1 nm. Higher magnification cannot reveal detail below the resolution limit; it only makes an unresolved image larger.

Microscopy using a beam of electrons instead of light. Its advantage is very much higher resolution and magnification, revealing ultrastructure such as ribosomes, membranes and the internal structure of organelles that a light microscope cannot resolve. Specimens must be dead, fixed, dehydrated and usually stained with heavy metals, and are viewed in a vacuum, so living cells cannot be observed and the images have no natural colour.

A technique in which a specimen is frozen very rapidly, then fractured with a blade. The fracture plane tends to run through the weak hydrophobic interior of membranes, between the two layers of the phospholipid bilayer. The exposed surfaces are coated with a thin layer of metal to make a replica, which is examined by electron microscopy. Freeze fracture revealed membrane proteins as particles embedded within the bilayer, which gave evidence for the fluid mosaic model.

Electron microscopy of specimens that have been frozen so rapidly that water solidifies as a glass-like solid without forming ice crystals, and are kept at very low temperature while being imaged. No chemical fixation or staining is needed, so molecules are preserved close to their natural state. Images of many identical molecules are combined by computer to produce three-dimensional structures of proteins and other large molecules at near-atomic resolution.

Dyes that absorb light of one wavelength and emit light of a longer wavelength. When a fluorescent stain that binds to a particular component, such as DNA, is used with a fluorescence light microscope, that component glows brightly against a dark background. Different fluorescent stains emitting different colours can be used together to show several components in the same cell.

A light microscopy technique in which antibodies that bind specifically to one protein are linked to a fluorescent marker. When the antibodies are applied to cells, the marker glows only where that protein is located, so the distribution of a single protein inside cells or tissues can be seen with a fluorescence microscope.

Typical cells of all living organisms have DNA as their genetic material, a cytoplasm composed mainly of water, and a plasma membrane composed of lipids. DNA stores the information for making the cell's proteins in a stable form that can be replicated and passed to daughter cells. Water is the solvent in which the reactions of metabolism take place and in which substances dissolve and move. Phospholipids have hydrophobic tails that form a bilayer barrier to water-soluble substances, so the membrane keeps the cell contents separate from the surroundings and controls what enters and leaves.

A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. The structure required is that of Gram-positive eubacteria such as Bacillus and Staphylococcus: a cell wall outside the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a single loop lying in the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells are typically about 1–10 µm in size and much smaller than most eukaryotic cells. Prokaryote cell structure varies between groups, but the details of the variations are not required.

DNA that is not associated with histone proteins. The DNA of a prokaryote is a single naked loop (a circular molecule) lying in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid; it is not enclosed by a membrane. 'Naked' refers to the absence of histones, not to the absence of a nuclear membrane.

The ribosomes of prokaryotic cells, which are smaller than the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm. The S value (Svedberg unit) describes the rate at which a particle sediments in a centrifuge and so reflects size. Prokaryotes carry out protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes; ribosomes are not membrane-bound, so their presence is consistent with the absence of membrane-bound organelles.

Bacteria such as Bacillus (rod-shaped) and Staphylococcus (spherical, in clusters) whose cell wall consists of a thick layer of peptidoglycan outside the plasma membrane. The cell wall of a prokaryote is not made of cellulose. These genera are the model for the prokaryotic cell structure required.

The organelle that contains the chromosomes of a eukaryotic cell. Each chromosome is a DNA molecule bound to histone proteins. The nucleus is enclosed by a double membrane (the nuclear envelope) that is perforated by nuclear pores, through which RNA and proteins pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.

The ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells, larger than the 70S ribosomes of prokaryotes. Some lie free in the cytoplasm and make proteins used within the cytoplasm; others are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, making it rough endoplasmic reticulum, and make proteins for secretion, for membranes or for lysosomes.

A network of protein fibres in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells, consisting of microtubules (hollow tubes of the protein tubulin) and microfilaments (thin fibres of the protein actin). The fibres are dynamic: they assemble and disassemble as needed to change cell shape, move organelles and vesicles, separate chromosomes during division and move cilia and flagella.

A vesicle bounded by a single membrane that contains hydrolytic enzymes. Lysosomes are one of the variety of vesicles found in eukaryotic cells; they digest material taken into the cell and break down worn-out organelles, keeping the enzymes separated from the rest of the cytoplasm.

A network of membrane tubules and flattened sacs continuous with the outer membrane of the nucleus. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has 80S ribosomes attached to its outer surface and synthesizes proteins that are transported in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus; smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and synthesizes lipids.

A stack of flattened, curved membrane sacs (cisternae), not studded with ribosomes, with vesicles budding from its edges. It receives proteins in vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and sorts them, and packages them into vesicles, including secretory vesicles that carry proteins to the plasma membrane for release.

An organelle bounded by a double membrane, the inner membrane being folded into cristae that project into a fluid matrix. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic cell respiration, producing ATP for the cell.

The processes that all living organisms, including unicellular organisms, carry out: homeostasis (keeping internal conditions within limits), metabolism (the enzyme-catalysed reactions of the cell, both synthesis and breakdown), nutrition (obtaining food or making it), movement, excretion (removal of the waste products of metabolism), growth, response to stimuli and reproduction. In a unicellular organism all of these are carried out within one cell.

Keeping the internal conditions of the cell within limits. In a freshwater unicellular organism such as Paramecium, water enters continuously by osmosis; a contractile vacuole collects this water and expels it from the cell, keeping the water content of the cytoplasm within limits. This is homeostasis, not excretion, because the water expelled is not a waste product of metabolism.

Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose; fungal cells have a cell wall made of chitin; animal cells have no cell wall. The cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and gives the cell strength and a fixed shape.

concepts.term: Vacuoles in animal, fungal and plant cells
concepts.def: Plant cells typically have a single large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, which stores substances and maintains the turgor pressure that supports the cell. Animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles, such as those formed when material is taken in by endocytosis. Fungal cells also have vacuoles.

A group of organelles found in plant cells but not in animal or fungal cells. Chloroplasts, the site of photosynthesis, are the best-known plastids, but there are others, such as amyloplasts that store starch and chromoplasts that contain pigments. Chloroplasts are present only in plant cells that are exposed to light, such as leaf cells, not in every plant cell.

Structures built from microtubules. Centrioles occur in pairs in animal cells and are involved in organizing the spindle during cell division; plant cells lack centrioles and still form a spindle. Cilia and flagella are projections from the cell surface that move the cell or move fluid past it; they are found in many animal cells and in some unicellular eukaryotes, but not in the cells of plants or fungi, with rare exceptions such as the swimming sperm of mosses and ferns.

Thread-like fungal filaments that are not divided by cross-walls (septa), so that many nuclei share one continuous cytoplasm. This arises because nuclei divide repeatedly without the cytoplasm being divided, giving one long multinucleate cell.

A very long muscle cell containing many nuclei. It forms during development by the fusion of many separate cells, so the nuclei of all of them lie within one plasma membrane, spread along the length of the fibre.

A mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleus: the nucleus is lost as the cell develops in the bone marrow, leaving more of the cell's volume for haemoglobin. Without a nucleus the cell cannot make new proteins or divide, and it has a limited lifespan.

A living plant cell in phloem that has lost its nucleus and most other organelles as it matured, leaving a cell with cytoplasm and a plasma membrane but no nucleus, through which sap can flow. It is kept alive by an adjacent companion cell, which retains its nucleus.

A prokaryotic cell is recognized by its small size, a cell wall, a nucleoid region of DNA not enclosed by a membrane, and the absence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. A plant cell is recognized by a cell wall, a large sap vacuole and, in photosynthetic cells, chloroplasts. An animal cell has no cell wall and no chloroplasts, may show microvilli, and has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

Nucleus: a large body bounded by a double membrane with pores, containing chromatin. Mitochondrion: a double membrane with the inner membrane folded into cristae. Chloroplast: a double membrane enclosing stacks of flattened thylakoids (grana). Rough endoplasmic reticulum: flattened sacs studded with ribosomes. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: tubules without ribosomes. Golgi apparatus: a discrete stack of curved, flattened sacs with vesicles budding from the edges and no ribosomes. Ribosomes: small dense granules. Sap vacuole: a large membrane-bound space in a plant cell. Microvilli: finger-like projections of the plasma membrane.

The region of the cytoplasm of a prokaryotic cell in which the naked DNA loop lies. In electron micrographs it appears as a paler, fibrous area not enclosed by a membrane, which distinguishes a prokaryote from a eukaryote with a membrane-bound nucleus.

A label on a drawing that gives information about the structure, in particular its function, rather than just its name. For example: rough endoplasmic reticulum — synthesizes proteins for secretion; Golgi apparatus — modifies proteins and packages them into vesicles; mitochondrion — site of aerobic cell respiration producing ATP; chloroplast — site of photosynthesis; sap vacuole — stores substances and maintains turgor; nucleus — contains the chromosomes and controls the cell's activities; plasma membrane — controls entry and exit of substances; cell wall — supports and protects the cell.

A small membrane-bound sac that buds from the Golgi apparatus carrying proteins to the plasma membrane. When it fuses with the plasma membrane its contents are released from the cell by exocytosis. Secretory vesicles differ from lysosomes, which contain hydrolytic enzymes and remain inside the cell.

Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane of some animal cells, such as those lining the small intestine, that greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Unlike cilia, microvilli do not beat or move.

The process by which mitochondria and, later in some lineages, chloroplasts originated: a prokaryotic cell was taken into a larger cell by endocytosis and, instead of being digested, survived and reproduced inside it, becoming an organelle. Evidence suggests all eukaryotes evolved from a common unicellular ancestor that already had a nucleus and reproduced sexually; mitochondria then evolved by endosymbiosis of an aerobic prokaryote, and in some eukaryotes chloroplasts subsequently arose by endosymbiosis of a photosynthetic prokaryote.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain naked circular DNA, like the DNA of prokaryotes; they contain 70S ribosomes, like prokaryotes, rather than the 80S ribosomes of the surrounding cytoplasm; and they replicate by dividing in two, independently of the division of the cell. They are also bounded by a double membrane, the inner membrane being derived from the plasma membrane of the engulfed prokaryote and the outer from the vesicle membrane of the host cell, and they are similar in size to prokaryotic cells.

The strength of a scientific theory comes from the range of observations it explains and the predictions it supports, not from direct observation of the events it proposes. The theory of endosymbiosis accounts for a wide range of observations about mitochondria and chloroplasts, and its predictions have been supported, which is why it is accepted even though the original endosymbiotic events happened over a billion years ago.

The process by which cells in a multicellular organism become specialized to form different tissues. Differentiated cells retain the whole genome; what differs between cell types is the pattern of gene expression, which determines which proteins are made and therefore the cell's structure and function.

The particular set of genes that is switched on in a cell. Different patterns of gene expression are the basis of differentiation, and they are often triggered by changes in the cell's environment, such as chemical signals from neighbouring cells or its position within the developing organism.

The condition of an organism consisting of many cells. Multicellularity has evolved repeatedly and independently in different eukaryotic lineages: many fungi and eukaryotic algae are multicellular, and all plants and animals are multicellular, while many other eukaryotes remain unicellular.

A multicellular organism can have a much larger body than a single cell, because each cell keeps a surface area to volume ratio adequate for exchange while the organism as a whole grows large. It also allows cell specialization: different cells differentiate to carry out different functions, which a single cell could not perform simultaneously and as efficiently.

mcqs.q: A biologist collects an organism from a deep-sea vent that has never been examined before. Before looking at it under a microscope, she predicts that it will consist of one or more cells. Which statement best describes this reasoning?
options: It is deductive: a specific prediction is derived from cell theory, and examining the organism then tests it.
It is inductive: the prediction is a generalization drawn from the many organisms already examined.
It is unscientific: cell theory cannot be relied on until every living organism has been examined.
It is unreliable: viruses are living organisms not made of cells, so cell theory has known exceptions.
mcqs.specStatementText: All living organisms are made of cells, so new ones can be predicted to be
mcqs.explain: Cell theory is a general theory; predicting that a particular new organism will consist of cells applies the theory to a specific case. This is deductive reasoning, and examining the organism tests the prediction, which is how a theory continues to be tested.
rationales: Cell theory is a general theory; predicting that a particular new organism will consist of cells applies the theory to a specific case. This is deductive reasoning, and examining the organism tests the prediction, which is how a theory continues to be tested.

A student who attaches 'inductive' to anything involving observations picks this. Induction built cell theory from many observations; using the theory to predict one new case runs the other way and is deduction.

A student who treats a theory as a guess until every case is checked picks this. A theory's value lies in generating predictions for cases not yet examined; the prediction is tested when the organism is examined.

A student who counts viruses as living organisms picks this. Viruses are not cells, have no metabolism and cannot reproduce independently, so they are not classified as living organisms and are not exceptions to cell theory.

mcqs.q: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?
options: 7.5 µm
mcqs.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
mcqs.explain: Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.
rationales: A student who multiplies the image size by the magnification picks this: 15 mm × 2000. That would make the real cell 30 m wide, larger than the image; actual size is image size divided by magnification.
Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.
A student who converts 0.0075 mm to micrometres using a factor of 100 picks this. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.0075 mm = 7.5 µm; a cell 0.75 µm across would be smaller than most bacteria.
A student who converts 0.0075 mm to micrometres using a factor of 10 picks this. 0.075 µm is 75 nm, about the size of a large virus; 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.0075 mm = 7.5 µm.

mcqs.q: With the ×40 objective lens in place, 40 divisions of an eyepiece graticule line up exactly with 100 µm on a stage micrometer. Using the same objective, a cell spans 44 graticule divisions. What is the actual length of the cell in millimetres?
options: 1.1 mm
mcqs.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
mcqs.explain: Calibration: 100 µm ÷ 40 divisions = 2.5 µm per division with this objective. The cell spans 44 divisions, so its length is 44 × 2.5 µm = 110 µm, which is 0.11 mm (1 mm = 1000 µm).
rationales: A student who assumes each graticule division is 1 µm, whatever the objective, takes the cell as 44 µm and converts that to 0.044 mm. The graticule has no fixed value; the stage micrometer shows each division is 2.5 µm here.

A student who applies the calibration the wrong way round, dividing 44 by 2.5 instead of multiplying by it, gets 17.6 µm and picks this. The calibration gives the actual length of one division, so the number of divisions is multiplied by it: 44 × 2.5 µm = 110 µm = 0.11 mm.
Calibration: 100 µm ÷ 40 divisions = 2.5 µm per division with this objective. The cell spans 44 divisions, so its length is 44 × 2.5 µm = 110 µm, which is 0.11 mm (1 mm = 1000 µm).
A student who obtains 110 µm and converts to millimetres using a factor of 100 picks this. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 110 µm ÷ 1000 = 0.11 mm; a cell 1.1 mm long would be visible to the naked eye.

mcqs.q: A student makes a drawing of a cell at a magnification of ×1250 and wants to add a scale bar representing 10 µm. How long should the scale bar be drawn?
options: 125 mm
10 mm
mcqs.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
mcqs.explain: The drawn length of a scale bar is the actual length it represents multiplied by the magnification: 10 µm × 1250 = 12 500 µm = 12.5 mm.
rationales: A student who divides by the magnification, as when finding an actual size, picks this: 10 µm ÷ 1250 = 0.008 µm. The scale bar is a magnified length, so the actual 10 µm is multiplied by 1250, not divided.
A student who calculates 12 500 µm and converts to millimetres using a factor of 100 picks this. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 12 500 µm ÷ 1000 = 12.5 mm, not 125 mm.

A student who reads the label's number as the drawn length picks this. The bar must be drawn at the actual length multiplied by the magnification: 10 µm × 1250 = 12 500 µm = 12.5 mm; a 10 mm bar would represent only 8 µm at ×1250.
The drawn length of a scale bar is the actual length it represents multiplied by the magnification: 10 µm × 1250 = 12 500 µm = 12.5 mm.

mcqs.q: A student focuses a stained temporary mount at low power, then rotates the high-power objective lens into place. The image is now slightly blurred. What should the student do?
options: Turn only the fine adjustment until the image is sharp.
Turn the coarse adjustment, since it changes the focus most quickly.
Add more stain to the mount so the structures show up clearly.
Switch to an even higher-power objective lens to enlarge the details.
mcqs.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
mcqs.explain: At high power the objective is close to the slide and the depth of focus is very small, so the fine adjustment is the only focusing control used; it moves the lens by tiny amounts to sharpen the image without risk to the slide or lens.
rationales: At high power the objective is close to the slide and the depth of focus is very small, so the fine adjustment is the only focusing control used; it moves the lens by tiny amounts to sharpen the image without risk to the slide or lens.

A student who uses the coarse adjustment for any blurred image picks this. At high power the coarse adjustment overshoots the focus and can drive the objective into the slide; it is used only at low power.
A student who credits the stain with sharpness picks this. Stain adds contrast between structures; it has no effect on focus, which is set by the distance between lens and specimen.
A student who thinks more magnification makes an image clearer picks this. Magnifying a blurred image gives a larger blurred image; the image must first be focused with the fine adjustment.

mcqs.q: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across. They cannot be seen with a light microscope but are clearly visible in electron micrographs. What is the reason?
options: The electron microscope magnifies many more times, so much smaller objects become visible.
Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.
Heavy-metal stains used for electron microscopy make small structures much sharper.
Electron microscopes use fluorescent stains that make ribosomes glow in the dark.
mcqs.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
mcqs.explain: Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used. Light limits a light microscope to about 200 nm, so a 25 nm ribosome cannot be resolved; the electron beam's much shorter wavelength gives resolution below 1 nm.
rationales: A student who explains everything by magnification picks this. Magnifying a light microscope image further would only enlarge the blur; without higher resolution, objects closer together than 200 nm remain indistinguishable.

Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used. Light limits a light microscope to about 200 nm, so a 25 nm ribosome cannot be resolved; the electron beam's much shorter wavelength gives resolution below 1 nm.
A student who credits stains with sharpness picks this. Stains add contrast by scattering electrons; they cannot reveal detail finer than the resolution of the microscope, which is set by wavelength.

A student who lumps all advanced techniques together picks this. Fluorescent stains are used in light microscopy, and they do not raise its resolution; ribosomes are resolved by the short wavelength of electrons.

mcqs.q: In freeze fracture, a rapidly frozen cell is split with a blade, the exposed surface is coated with metal, and the replica is examined by electron microscopy. Replicas of plasma membranes show a smooth face scattered with small bumps. What does this show?
options: The fracture cut straight across the cell, and the bumps are organelles seen in cross-section.
Ice crystals grew inside the membrane as it froze, and the bumps are the crystals left in the replica.
The fracture ran between the two phospholipid layers, and the bumps are proteins embedded within the bilayer.
The fracture exposed the outer surface, and the bumps are the protein coat covering the bilayer.
mcqs.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
mcqs.explain: The weakest plane in a frozen membrane is the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer, so the fracture splits the membrane into its two layers. Proteins embedded in the bilayer are left standing as bumps, which was evidence for the fluid mosaic model.
rationales: A student who pictures fracturing as cutting a section picks this. The fracture follows the weakest plane, inside membranes, rather than crossing them; the replica shows a membrane face, not a section.
A student who assumes freezing always forms ice crystals picks this. The cell is frozen so rapidly that no crystals form, which is what preserves the membrane structure for fracturing.

The weakest plane in a frozen membrane is the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer, so the fracture splits the membrane into its two layers. Proteins embedded in the bilayer are left standing as bumps, which was evidence for the fluid mosaic model.

A student who pictures the membrane as a lipid layer coated with protein picks this. The fracture exposes the interior of the bilayer, and the particles are proteins embedded within it, not a coat on its surface.

mcqs.q: A researcher wants to see where one particular protein is located inside cultured cells. Which approach will show this?
options: A general stain such as methylene blue, which binds to proteins so that every location of the protein is coloured.
A higher-power objective lens, since enough magnification will show which structures contain the protein.
Transmission electron microscopy of the living cells, since its resolution is high enough to show single protein molecules.
Immunofluorescence: antibodies that bind only that protein carry a fluorescent marker seen with a light microscope.
mcqs.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
mcqs.explain: Antibodies bind specifically to one protein. Linking them to a fluorescent marker makes that protein, and only that protein, glow under a fluorescence microscope, revealing where it is in the cell.
rationales: A student who thinks all stains work like methylene blue picks this. A general stain colours many components of the cell at once and cannot distinguish one protein from all the others.

A student who expects magnification to reveal anything picks this. Magnification does not distinguish one protein from another, and resolution, not magnification, limits what a light microscope can show.
A student who thinks electron microscopes view living cells picks this. Specimens must be dead, fixed and in a vacuum, and even at high resolution one unlabelled protein cannot be told from another.
Antibodies bind specifically to one protein. Linking them to a fluorescent marker makes that protein, and only that protein, glow under a fluorescence microscope, revealing where it is in the cell.

mcqs.q: What is the main advantage of cryogenic electron microscopy over conventional electron microscopy?
options: Rapid freezing keeps unfixed, unstained molecules near their natural state, so structures are resolved in near-atomic detail.
Heavy-metal stains bind more firmly at very low temperature, so the contrast between structures in the specimen is much greater.
Freezing makes the cell brittle, so it can be fractured to reveal the interior of its membranes in section.
The very low temperature prevents the electron beam from killing the cells, so living cells can be observed in action.
mcqs.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
mcqs.explain: Plunge-freezing solidifies the water without ice crystals, so no fixation or staining is needed and molecules keep their natural shape. Combining images of many identical molecules gives three-dimensional structures of proteins at near-atomic resolution.
rationales: Plunge-freezing solidifies the water without ice crystals, so no fixation or staining is needed and molecules keep their natural shape. Combining images of many identical molecules gives three-dimensional structures of proteins at near-atomic resolution.

A student who assumes cryogenic specimens still need staining picks this. The point of the technique is that no stain or fixative is used, so molecules are seen as they are rather than as a stain outlines them.

A student who confuses cryogenic electron microscopy with freeze fracture picks this. Fracturing frozen cells to expose membrane interiors is freeze fracture; cryogenic electron microscopy images the frozen specimen directly.

A student who thinks electron microscopy can be made to work on living cells picks this. A vitrified specimen at very low temperature in a vacuum is not alive; the advantage is structural preservation, not life.

mcqs.q: Every living cell has DNA as genetic material, a cytoplasm composed mainly of water, and a plasma membrane composed of lipids. Which statement gives a correct reason for one of these features?
options: The cytoplasm is mainly water so that it forms a stiff gel that holds every organelle in a fixed position.
The membrane is made of lipids because their hydrophobic tails form a barrier to the water-soluble contents of the cell.
The membrane is made of lipids because lipids form a rigid layer that gives the cell its strength and shape.
DNA is the genetic material because it is protected inside a nucleus in every kind of living cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: What every cell has, and why
mcqs.explain: Phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer with their hydrophobic tails inward. The hydrophobic interior blocks the passage of water-soluble substances, so the membrane keeps the aqueous cytoplasm separate from the surroundings and controls exchange.
rationales: A student who pictures cytoplasm as a solid jelly picks this. Cytoplasm is mainly water because water is the solvent for metabolism; organelles move within it and are positioned by the cytoskeleton.

Phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer with their hydrophobic tails inward. The hydrophobic interior blocks the passage of water-soluble substances, so the membrane keeps the aqueous cytoplasm separate from the surroundings and controls exchange.

A student who gives the membrane the role of a wall picks this. The phospholipid bilayer is fluid and flexible; it is a barrier, not a support. Strength and shape come from a cell wall, where present, or the cytoskeleton.

A student who thinks every cell has a nucleus picks this. Prokaryotes keep their DNA in the cytoplasm without a nucleus; DNA is the genetic material because it stores information stably and can be replicated.

mcqs.q: Which description of the structure of a Bacillus cell is correct?
options: The DNA is enclosed by a nuclear membrane inside a small nucleus within the cytoplasm.
The cell wall outside the plasma membrane is built from long parallel fibres of cellulose.
A loop of naked DNA lies in the cytoplasm, and proteins are made on 70S ribosomes.
The DNA loop is wound around histone proteins to package it within the nucleoid region.
mcqs.specStatementText: Prokaryotic cell structure
mcqs.explain: A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesized.
rationales: A student who expects every cell to have a nucleus picks this. Prokaryotic DNA lies in the cytoplasm in a nucleoid region that is not enclosed by any membrane.
A student who assumes every cell wall is a cellulose wall picks this. The cell wall of Bacillus is made of peptidoglycan; cellulose walls are found only in plant cells.

A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesized.
A student who thinks 'naked' refers only to the absence of a membrane picks this. Naked DNA is DNA not associated with histones; the prokaryotic loop has no histones.

mcqs.q: A unicellular organism is found to have a cell wall, a plasma membrane and ribosomes, but no nucleus. Its DNA is a single circular molecule, not associated with histones, lying in the cytoplasm. A student concludes that the organism is a prokaryote. Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?
options: It is wrong: the presence of a cell wall means the organism must be either a plant or a fungus.
It is wrong: prokaryotes are too simple to have ribosomes, so this must be a eukaryote.
It is wrong: every cell has a nucleus, so the DNA must lie in a nucleus that was overlooked.
It is justified: naked circular DNA in the cytoplasm with no nucleus is a prokaryotic feature.
mcqs.specStatementText: Prokaryotic cell structure
mcqs.explain: DNA in a single naked loop lying in the cytoplasm, with no nucleus, is characteristic of prokaryotes. The cell wall and ribosomes are consistent with this but do not decide it, since eukaryotes may have both.
rationales: A student who treats a cell wall as a eukaryotic feature picks this. Prokaryotes also have cell walls, so the wall does not rule out a prokaryote; the naked DNA without a nucleus is decisive.
A student who thinks ribosomes are eukaryotic organelles picks this. Every living cell has ribosomes; prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes and make all their proteins on them.
A student who believes a nucleus is universal picks this. Prokaryotes have no nucleus; their DNA lies in the cytoplasm, exactly as described, so nothing was overlooked.

DNA in a single naked loop lying in the cytoplasm, with no nucleus, is characteristic of prokaryotes. The cell wall and ribosomes are consistent with this but do not decide it, since eukaryotes may have both.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the structure of a eukaryotic cell is correct?
options: The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane with pores, and its DNA is bound to histone proteins.
The nucleus is enclosed by a single membrane that is continuous with the plasma membrane.
The ribosomes in the cytoplasm are 70S, the same size as those found in bacteria.
The cytoskeleton is a rigid, permanent frame of protein rods holding each organelle in a fixed position.
mcqs.specStatementText: Eukaryotic cell structure
mcqs.explain: The eukaryotic nucleus is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane perforated by pores, and contains chromosomes consisting of DNA bound to histones.
rationales: The eukaryotic nucleus is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane perforated by pores, and contains chromosomes consisting of DNA bound to histones.
A student who pictures every organelle with one outline picks this. The nuclear envelope is a double membrane with pores; it is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum, not the plasma membrane.
A student who thinks all ribosomes are alike picks this. The ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm are 80S; 70S ribosomes are found in prokaryotes and inside mitochondria and chloroplasts.
A student led by the word 'skeleton' picks this. Microtubules and microfilaments are dynamic, assembling and disassembling to move organelles, change cell shape and form the spindle.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes a membrane-bound organelle of a eukaryotic cell?
options: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened sacs studded with ribosomes that synthesize proteins.
Lysosomes are vesicles bounded by a single membrane that contain hydrolytic enzymes.
Mitochondria are bounded by a single membrane folded inward to form cristae.
Secretory vesicles are lysosomes under another name, digesting worn-out organelles.
mcqs.specStatementText: Eukaryotic cell structure
mcqs.explain: Lysosomes are one of the variety of vesicles in eukaryotic cells: single-membrane sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes, kept separate from the rest of the cytoplasm, that digest material taken in and worn-out organelles.
rationales: A student who merges the Golgi apparatus with rough endoplasmic reticulum picks this. The Golgi apparatus has no ribosomes; it modifies and packages proteins that were synthesized on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

Lysosomes are one of the variety of vesicles in eukaryotic cells: single-membrane sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes, kept separate from the rest of the cytoplasm, that digest material taken in and worn-out organelles.
A student who gives every organelle one membrane picks this. A mitochondrion has a double membrane; it is the inner of the two that is folded into cristae.

A student who treats every small vesicle as a lysosome picks this. Secretory vesicles carry products from the Golgi apparatus to the plasma membrane for release by exocytosis; lysosomes are a different kind of vesicle that digests material inside the cell.

mcqs.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Which statement correctly identifies one of its functions of life?
options: Growth: dividing by binary fission, so that the single cell becomes two separate cells.
Excretion: a process not carried out, because removing metabolic waste requires organs such as kidneys.
Homeostasis: expelling water that enters by osmosis, keeping the water content of the cytoplasm within limits.
Metabolism: releasing energy from food by respiration, without building up any new molecules.
mcqs.specStatementText: One cell can carry out every function of life
mcqs.explain: Water enters continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it, keeping the internal water content within limits. The water is not a product of metabolism, so this is homeostasis rather than excretion.
rationales: A student who sees division as the organism getting bigger picks this. In a unicellular organism the cell is the organism, so division produces two organisms: that is reproduction. Growth is the increase in cell size between divisions.

A student who ties excretion to organs picks this. A single cell must carry out every function of life; the waste products of its metabolism, such as carbon dioxide, leave by diffusion across the plasma membrane.

Water enters continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it, keeping the internal water content within limits. The water is not a product of metabolism, so this is homeostasis rather than excretion.

A student who uses the everyday meaning of metabolism picks this. Metabolism is all the enzyme-catalysed reactions of the cell, including the synthesis of proteins and other molecules as well as respiration.

mcqs.q: Which row correctly compares the cells of animals, fungi and plants?
options: Cell wall: absent in animals, made of cellulose in fungi, made of cellulose in plants.
Vacuoles: absent in animals, present in fungi, present as a large sap vacuole in plants.
Centrioles: present in animals, absent in fungi, present in plants to form the spindle.
Cell wall: absent in animals, made of chitin in fungi, made of cellulose in plants.
mcqs.specStatementText: How animal, fungal and plant cells differ
mcqs.explain: Animal cells have no cell wall. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and plant cell walls of cellulose; the presence and composition of the wall is one of the main differences between the three groups.
rationales: A student who groups fungi with plants picks this. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose; only plant cells have cellulose walls.

A student who remembers 'vacuole: plants only' picks this. Animal cells have small temporary vacuoles; the difference from the large permanent sap vacuole of plant cells is in size and function, not presence.
A student who thinks a spindle needs centrioles picks this. Plant cells lack centrioles and organize their spindle without them; centrioles are a feature of animal cells.

Animal cells have no cell wall. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and plant cell walls of cellulose; the presence and composition of the wall is one of the main differences between the three groups.

mcqs.q: A cell taken from a multicellular organism has a cell wall, a nucleus, no chloroplasts and no centrioles. A student concludes that it must be a fungal cell. Is this conclusion justified?
options: No: a plant root cell also fits every feature listed, and the composition of the wall would decide between them.
No: fungal and plant cell walls are both made of cellulose, so the composition of the wall cannot help to decide either.
Yes: every plant cell contains chloroplasts, so the absence of chloroplasts rules out a plant cell.
Yes: plant cells need centrioles to form a spindle, so a walled cell without any centrioles cannot be a plant cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: How animal, fungal and plant cells differ
mcqs.explain: Plant cells lack centrioles, and plant cells that are not exposed to light have no chloroplasts, so a root cell matches every feature listed. A chitin wall would indicate a fungus and a cellulose wall a plant.
rationales: Plant cells lack centrioles, and plant cells that are not exposed to light have no chloroplasts, so a root cell matches every feature listed. A chitin wall would indicate a fungus and a cellulose wall a plant.
A student who thinks fungi have cellulose walls picks this. Fungal walls are made of chitin and plant walls of cellulose, so the composition of the wall is exactly what distinguishes them.
A student who takes the leaf cell as the model for all plant cells picks this. Root cells and many other plant cells have no chloroplasts, so their absence does not rule out a plant.
A student who believes a spindle requires centrioles picks this. Plant cells have no centrioles and still form a spindle, so the absence of centrioles is consistent with a plant cell.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the number of nuclei in an atypical eukaryotic cell?
options: A mature red blood cell keeps a single nucleus so that it can control the making of haemoglobin.
An aseptate fungal hypha contains many nuclei within one continuous cytoplasm.
A skeletal muscle fibre has a single, very large nucleus to control its whole length.
A phloem sieve tube element is a dead cell, so it has no nucleus and no cytoplasm.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells that break the one-nucleus rule
mcqs.explain: Aseptate hyphae have no cross-walls, so repeated nuclear division without division of the cytoplasm leaves many nuclei sharing a single continuous cytoplasm inside one plasma membrane.
rationales: A student who assumes a protein-filled cell must be making protein picks this. The haemoglobin was made before the nucleus was lost; a mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleus.
Aseptate hyphae have no cross-walls, so repeated nuclear division without division of the cytoplasm leaves many nuclei sharing a single continuous cytoplasm inside one plasma membrane.
A student who holds to one nucleus per cell picks this. A skeletal muscle fibre forms by the fusion of many cells and so contains many nuclei spread along its length.

A student who models phloem on xylem picks this. A sieve tube element is alive, with cytoplasm and a plasma membrane; it is atypical because it has lost its nucleus at maturity, and is supported by a companion cell.

mcqs.q: An electron micrograph shows a cell about 3 µm long. It has a cell wall, a paler fibrous region of DNA not enclosed by any membrane, many small dense granules, and no membrane-bound organelles. How should the cell be classified?
options: As a plant cell, because a cell wall is found only around the cells of plants.
As a eukaryote, because the region containing DNA must be a nucleus, as every cell has one.
As a prokaryote, because its DNA lies in a nucleoid region and it has no membrane-bound organelles.
As a eukaryote, because prokaryotic cells are too simple to contain any ribosomes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
mcqs.explain: A nucleoid region of DNA without a membrane, the absence of membrane-bound organelles and the small size identify a prokaryote; the granules are 70S ribosomes and the cell wall is consistent with a bacterium.
rationales: A student who takes a cell wall to mean 'plant' picks this. Prokaryotes and fungi also have cell walls; a plant cell would show a nucleus, a sap vacuole and other membrane-bound organelles.

A student who believes every cell has a nucleus reads the nucleoid as a nucleus. A nucleus is bounded by a double membrane; DNA lying in the cytoplasm with no membrane is a nucleoid, a prokaryotic feature.

A nucleoid region of DNA without a membrane, the absence of membrane-bound organelles and the small size identify a prokaryote; the granules are 70S ribosomes and the cell wall is consistent with a bacterium.
A student who counts ribosomes as eukaryotic organelles picks this. All cells have ribosomes; the small dense granules are the 70S ribosomes of a prokaryote.

mcqs.q: In an electron micrograph of an animal cell, a structure appears as a discrete stack of curved, flattened membrane sacs with small vesicles budding from its edges and no ribosomes attached. Which structure is it?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, where lipids are made
Mitochondrion, where aerobic cell respiration is carried out
Rough endoplasmic reticulum, where secreted proteins are made
Golgi apparatus, where proteins are modified and packaged
mcqs.specStatementText: Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
mcqs.explain: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of curved cisternae, separate from the nuclear envelope, with no ribosomes on its surface and vesicles budding from its edges as proteins are packaged for transport.
rationales: A student who identifies any membrane sacs as endoplasmic reticulum and then decides by the absence of ribosomes picks this. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a network of tubules, not a discrete curved stack with budding vesicles.

A student who labels any structure with internal membranes as a mitochondrion picks this. A mitochondrion is enclosed by a double membrane with the inner membrane folded into cristae; it is not an open stack of sacs shedding vesicles.

A student who takes 'rough' to mean the folded texture of the membranes picks this. Rough endoplasmic reticulum is identified by attached ribosomes, which are absent here; a ribosome-free stack of curved sacs with budding vesicles is the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi apparatus is a stack of curved cisternae, separate from the nuclear envelope, with no ribosomes on its surface and vesicles budding from its edges as proteins are packaged for transport.

mcqs.q: A student draws a cell from an electron micrograph of a gland that secretes enzymes, and must annotate each structure with its function. Which annotation is correct?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum — synthesizes proteins that are destined for secretion from the cell.
Golgi apparatus — synthesizes the enzymes that the cell will later secrete by exocytosis.
Microvilli — beat rhythmically to move the secreted enzymes along the surface of the cell.
Secretory vesicles — break down worn-out organelles inside the cell using the hydrolytic enzymes they hold.
mcqs.specStatementText: Drawing and annotating cell structures from micrographs
mcqs.explain: Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesize proteins for secretion, which pass into the reticulum and are carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, then to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles.
rationales: Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesize proteins for secretion, which pass into the reticulum and are carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, then to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles.
A student who gives the Golgi apparatus the job of protein synthesis picks this. Proteins are synthesized only on ribosomes; the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them into vesicles.
A student who confuses microvilli with cilia picks this. Microvilli are static folds of the plasma membrane that increase surface area; they do not beat.

A student who treats all small vesicles as lysosomes picks this. Secretory vesicles carry the cell's products to the plasma membrane for release by exocytosis; digestion of organelles is the role of lysosomes.

mcqs.q: If mitochondria originated as free-living prokaryotes taken into a larger cell, which features would the theory of endosymbiosis predict mitochondria to have?
options: Ribosomes identical to those of the cytoplasm, because the host cell now makes them all.
Naked circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, with the ability to divide independently of the host cell.
DNA wound around histone proteins, because all DNA in the cell is packaged in that way.
A double membrane in which both layers are derived from the vesicle membrane of the host cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes
mcqs.explain: A former prokaryote should retain prokaryotic features: naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and replication by dividing in two. Mitochondria show all three, which is the evidence the guide specifies for endosymbiosis.
rationales: A student who thinks all ribosomes are the same picks this. Mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S, like those of prokaryotes, not the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm, which is a key piece of evidence.

A former prokaryote should retain prokaryotic features: naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and replication by dividing in two. Mitochondria show all three, which is the evidence the guide specifies for endosymbiosis.
A student who believes histones are universal picks this. Prokaryotic DNA is naked, and so is mitochondrial DNA; if mitochondria had histone-bound DNA it would count against a prokaryotic origin.
A student who forgets the engulfed cell had its own membrane picks this. The inner membrane is the former prokaryote's plasma membrane; only the outer membrane came from the host vesicle.

mcqs.q: Evidence suggests that all eukaryotes evolved from a common unicellular ancestor that had a nucleus, that mitochondria then evolved by endosymbiosis, and that in some eukaryotes chloroplasts subsequently also had an endosymbiotic origin. Which conclusion is consistent with this evidence and with the nature of scientific theories?
options: The earliest eukaryotes were photosynthetic, and lineages such as animals and fungi have since lost their chloroplasts.
The nucleus itself arose when an early cell engulfed a prokaryote, in the same way as mitochondria arose.
The ancestors of plants already had mitochondria when a photosynthetic prokaryote was taken in as a chloroplast.
Because the engulfing events were not observed, endosymbiosis remains a weak theory with little supporting evidence.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes
mcqs.explain: Mitochondria were acquired before the eukaryote lineages diverged, and chloroplasts were acquired later in only some lineages, so the cell that took in the future chloroplast already contained mitochondria. This explains why plants have both organelles and animals only mitochondria.
rationales: A student who assumes producers came first at every level picks this. Chloroplasts arose after mitochondria and only in some lineages; there is no evidence that animals or fungi ever possessed them.

A student who extends endosymbiosis to every double-membraned structure picks this. The common ancestor already had a nucleus before mitochondria were acquired, and the nucleus lacks the prokaryotic features seen in mitochondria.

Mitochondria were acquired before the eukaryote lineages diverged, and chloroplasts were acquired later in only some lineages, so the cell that took in the future chloroplast already contained mitochondria. This explains why plants have both organelles and animals only mitochondria.

A student who takes 'theory' to mean speculation picks this. A theory's strength comes from the observations it explains and the predictions it supports, and endosymbiosis accounts for a wide range of observations about mitochondria and chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: A muscle cell and a neurone from the same person contain the same genome, yet they differ greatly in structure and function. What is the basis of this difference?
options: Each cell has kept only the genes it needs and has lost the genes for the other cell type.
Each cell's fate was fixed at fertilization by its genes alone, with no influence from its surroundings.
Mutations that accumulated in each cell type during development altered the DNA sequence differently.
Different sets of genes are expressed in each cell, often triggered by its environment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells specialize by expressing different genes
mcqs.explain: Differentiation is based on different patterns of gene expression: the same genome is present, but each cell type expresses a different set of genes, and these patterns are often triggered by changes in the environment of the cell, such as signals from neighbouring cells.
rationales: A student who explains permanent differentiation by loss of genes picks this. Differentiated cells keep the whole genome; the unused genes are present but not expressed.

A student who thinks genes act independently of the environment picks this. Since every cell has the same genes, it is signals from each cell's surroundings that trigger the different patterns of expression.

A student who knows only mutation as a way of changing a cell picks this. The DNA sequence is the same in both cells; what differs is which genes are switched on, which is controlled without changing the sequence.

Differentiation is based on different patterns of gene expression: the same genome is present, but each cell type expresses a different set of genes, and these patterns are often triggered by changes in the environment of the cell, such as signals from neighbouring cells.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the evolution of multicellularity is correct?
options: Multicellularity evolved independently in several eukaryotic lineages, including plants, animals and fungi.
Multicellularity evolved only once, so all multicellular organisms descend from a single multicellular ancestor.
Unicellular eukaryotes are transitional forms that will become multicellular given enough time.
Larger body size could be reached equally well by one cell growing larger, so specialization is the only real advantage.
mcqs.specStatementText: Multicellularity evolved many times and brings two advantages
mcqs.explain: Multicellularity has evolved repeatedly: the closest relatives of plants, of animals and of fungi are unicellular, and several unrelated groups of algae are also multicellular. All plants and animals, and many fungi and eukaryotic algae, are multicellular.
rationales: Multicellularity has evolved repeatedly: the closest relatives of plants, of animals and of fungi are unicellular, and several unrelated groups of algae are also multicellular. All plants and animals, and many fungi and eukaryotic algae, are multicellular.

A student who models multicellularity on features that arose once, such as mitochondria, picks this. Plants, animals, fungi and several algal groups each became multicellular separately from unicellular ancestors.
A student who pictures evolution as a ladder of progress picks this. Evolution has no goal; unicellular eukaryotes are abundant and successful, and most eukaryotic lineages have remained unicellular.

A student who imagines a body scaled up as a single cell picks this. A cell's surface area to volume ratio falls as it grows, limiting its size; multicellularity allows a large body made of small cells, as well as specialization.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic A2.2 Cell structure

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Prokaryote structure is presented only as that of Gram-positive eubacteria such as Bacillus and Staphylococcus (cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop, 70S ribosomes), with a single sentence noting that prokaryote structure varies. No item, concept or misconception mentions mycoplasmas, phytoplasmas, Gram-negative wall structure, or prokaryotic capsules, pili, flagella or plasmids; the only cilia and flagella in the file are the eukaryotic structures required by A2.2.8.
